sections.html: Omobranchus belongs to the Blenniidae family, most of which live in marine environments. There are only very few species that settle permanently in fresh or brackish water. The maximum size is around 7 cm.
The species has a large distribution along the coastline of the Indo-West-Pacific, ranging from the Bay of Bengal in the west to Singapore in the east.

The fish are found almost exclusively in brackish and fresh water, although they are said to tolerate also pure marine water. They breed in the mangrove area in holes in the bottom. The larvae develop in the sea.

The specimens have proved so far to be very lively and healthy, even without adding salt. The photographed specimens for example stayed about ten days in the photo tank in pure freshwater to settle themselves and obviously felt very well. Nevertheless a slight addition of salt – about 5 g/l – is suggested. If salt is used over a long period, commercially manufactured sea salt for coral fish aquaria is recommended.
The fish feed readily on all usual types of food for ornamental fishes. In nature, these fishes are carnivorous and feed on small invertebrates.
Like all blennies, these fishes defend a small territory, but neither conspecifics nor tankmates belonging to other species become hurt usually.

Males and females have a similar coloration, but the dorsal fin and the lateral spots are more intensively colored in males. The easiest detectable sexual dimorphism can be found in the structure of the anal fin. In this fin the male's anterior four rays are flattened on the tip. Besides this the males become larger than the females. There are a lot of additional sexual dimorphisms; the paper by Springer & Gomon (1975) is recommended for those with a special interest.

Springer, V. G. & M. F. Gomon (1975): Revision of the blenniid fish genus Omobranchus with descriptions of three new species and notes on other species of the tribe Omobranchini. Smithonian contributions to zoology 177.
